place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆 · 十一月

setup.zh: 院系杯小组赛，他抢到头一个篮板，落地崴了右脚。针灸实验课上他头一个举手得气，严老师却说：「疼和伤，是两本账。」阿禾单脚闭眼站给他看：崴过脚的，都得练这个。
setup.en: The group stage of the cup: his first rebound, and he lands on his right ankle. In the acupuncture practical he is first to volunteer and feels the qi arrive, but Teacher Yan says: "Pain and injury are two separate accounts." Ahe stands on one foot, eyes shut, to show him: everyone who sprains an ankle has to do this.

recap.zh: 崴了右踝；针灸课得气、老蔡晕针；「疼和伤，是两本账」；单脚闭眼，三秒。
recap.en: A sprained right ankle; deqi in the needling class and Old Cai fainting; "pain and injury are two accounts"; one foot, eyes shut, three seconds.

en: One foot, eyes shut: three seconds.

story.zh:
十一月二十五日夜里十一点，沈芒看着马桶里一泡可乐色的尿，头一个念头不是「我要死了」，是：不许让阿禾知道。

这句话，四天前他就对自己说过一回。

十一月十四日，星期六，院系杯小组赛第二轮，针推对护理。

第二节打到一半，阿禾在记分台后头翻了一页本子，跟队长邢斌说了句什么。邢斌冲板凳一招手：「零号。」

五分钟。她说话算话。

沈芒站起来的时候，两条腿是软的；一上场，倒不软了——护理学院的人一个比一个高，可他们打球的样子，比他还怕球。头两分钟他跟着球跑，球到哪儿他到哪儿，像一条追着自己尾巴转的狗。第三分钟，护理那个最高的大个子在罚球线附近出手，球砸在篮筐后沿上，弹得老高。

篮下一群人一齐跳起来。沈芒也跳了。他也不知道哪儿来的胆子，跟着一群比他高半个头的人一齐跳，两只手往天上一够——球竟然砸在了他手上。他把它搂进了怀里。

院系杯的头一个篮板。

落地的时候，他的右脚没落在地板上，落在了那个大个子的脚面上。脚踝往外一翻，「咯」的一声，他自己都听见了。

然后是疼。疼得他眼前一白，抱着球坐在了地上。球还死死地搂在怀里，谁来掰都不撒手。疼归疼，他胸口有一样东西在烧，烧得眼泪都顶出来了——抢着了。院系杯的头一个篮板，是零号的。他抬头往记分台那边看了一眼，阿禾正低着头写字，没看他。

针推那天赢了护理九分。他没看见终场——阿禾叫两个替补架着他，直接去了校门口的校医院，她自己跟在后头，本子夹在胳膊底下。

校医院的大夫捏了捏他的脚踝，又按了按外踝骨头的边上，让他扶着墙走了四步：「骨头按着不怎么疼，先不拍片。外踝的韧带拉伤了。」开了一副护踝，一对拐。沈芒问：「几天能好？」校医说：「一两个礼拜就不疼了。要长结实，少说三个月。」

他只听进去了前半句：第三轮在一个礼拜以后，不疼就能上。

阿禾听进去的是后半句。她问大夫：「头几天冰不冰？几天能落地？要不要拍片？」一样一样问完了，在本子上写了一行。出了校医院，沈芒拄着拐追上她：「第三轮——」

「校医说三个月。」阿禾说，「我写了。」

他想问写的什么，拐先在台阶上打了个滑。

十一月十七日，星期二上午，实验楼三楼，针灸实验课。

严老师的白大褂照旧扣到最上面一颗扣子。课表上写得明明白白：「腧穴定位与毫针刺法练习（足三里）」。两人一组，先在自己腿上找穴；针不往人身上扎，往纸垫、棉团上扎，练指力，练进针；末了，严老师找一个志愿者，在腿上扎一回足三里，做示范。

沈芒拄着拐进门，心里揣着一个主意。针灸不就是治这个的吗？校医院推拿科门口那块牌子上，「踝关节扭伤」写得清清楚楚。今天严老师找志愿者，他头一个举手；针扎进去，说不定连脚踝一块儿通了，礼拜六就能上。

他跟老蔡一组。

严老师先讲定位：膝盖底下外侧那个凹窝往下三寸，胫骨前缘往外一横指。全班低着头在自己腿上摸，摸得一片「哎哟」。沈芒背书背不下来，这个倒摸着了——他把指头按在胫骨外边那条肉上，脚尖一勾，那条肉在他指头底下一鼓。解剖课上这条肌肉有名字，胫骨前肌。穴位就在这条肉上，旁边一条神经、一条血管从深处走过去。他忽然觉得，这些穴位倒不全是天上掉下来的：不少落在神经、血管经过的地方，或是筋肉之间的缝里——那是人伸手摸得着的东西。

「足三里，胃经的合穴。」严老师拿粉笔点着黑板上那张腿，「从指尖、脚尖往上到肘、膝，每条经上排着五个要穴：井、荥、输、经、合。像水从泉眼里冒出来，流成小沟，汇成河，末了入海。合，就是入海的地方。为什么这么排，下学期经络腧穴学细讲。」

老蔡低头瞅着自己的小腿：「我腿里有海？」

全班笑了。严老师没笑，也没骂，接着发针。纸垫是一叠草纸拿线捆紧的，捏着针柄，一捻一捻往里送；扎透了，换棉团，练进针要快、要直。老蔡在对面捏着一根针，手抖得像在给针尖跳舞，捻了半天，针在纸垫上弯成了一张弓。沈芒的针倒是直的——他在手机上刷过一个月扎针的视频，手上有点样子。

末了，严老师道：「谁来？」

沈芒的手头一个举了起来。他拄着拐坐上实验床，撩起裤腿。严老师消了毒，一针进去，快得他没看清。腿上一酸，跟着一胀，一股说不清的麻，顺着小腿往下走。

「得气了。」严老师对全班说，「酸、胀、麻，往下走。扎针要的就是这个。」

老蔡在旁边两眼放光：「忙哥！什么感觉？」

「酸。」

第二个举手的是老蔡。他说他也要亲身体会一回。他在实验床上坐好，严老师的针刚碰着皮，老蔡的脸先白了，额头上一层冷汗，身子一软，往旁边就倒。严老师一个箭步把他放平，两条腿垫高，开窗，叫人拿糖水。过了几分钟，老蔡的脸色回来了，躺在床沿上，有气无力地说：「……我早饭没吃。」

「晕针。」严老师对全班说，「空着肚子、累着、紧张，最容易。所以扎针前要吃饭，躺着扎比坐着扎稳当。」这是书上的话，他一个字不差地念了；念完又补了一句书上没有的，「你们以后给病人扎，也一样。」

下课前，沈芒拄着拐蹭到讲台边，撩起裤腿，露出肿得像发面馒头的脚踝：「严老师，给我这儿扎两针，礼拜六能上场吗？」

严老师看了一会儿，没马上答。他回身在黑板上写了一行：「[所言节者，神气之所游行出入也，非皮肉筋骨也。]{典=lingshu-jiuzhen}」写完拿粉笔头点着念了一遍：「《灵枢》头一篇。节，就是后来说的穴。古人说，它不是皮、肉、筋、骨，是神气出入的地方。神气是什么，书上没写，我也不替它写。」

沈芒的指头还按在小腿上。书上说不是肉；他指头底下，分明是肉。

「扎针，对一部分疼是有用的。」严老师合上教材，「可有人拿不扎进去的假针跟真针比过，差得常常不大。它为什么管用，有好几种说法，哪一种都没定论。」他看了看表，离下课还有十分钟，「躺上来。扎给你们看看。」

全班呼啦一下围了上来。沈芒躺上实验床，裤腿撩到膝盖。严老师没碰那只脚踝，先拿起他的左手。

「崴的是右脚，我先扎左手。」他拿拇指在沈芒手腕背面那道横纹正中按了按，「阳池。手少阳经的穴，腕子对着脚踝——手上这个关节，跟脚上那个是对着的。老规矩叫左病右取，远处先扎一针，疼的地方先不碰。」消毒，一针进去，沈芒「嘶」了一声。「酸不酸？」「酸。」「酸着。现在，右脚踝慢慢转圈。不许快，疼就停。」

沈芒躺着，架着那只肿脚踝，一圈一圈地转。头几圈像拧一把生锈的锁，转到第七八圈，锁里头那股涩，松了一点点。他自己觉出来了，脸上大概也带出来了，严老师点点头：「转的时候针留着，叫运动针法。效果就这么一点点，不是神仙水。」

针起了。严老师这才低头看那只脚踝，拿两根指头隔着肿的地方比划：「外踝前头、底下，肿得最高的地方，是距腓前韧带，崴脚十回有八回撕的是它。肿着，不往里扎。扎它周围。」他一边说一边下针，针都浅，捻两下就停：外踝前下方那个凹里一针，「丘墟」；外踝后头、跟腱前头那个窝里一针，「昆仑」；外踝正底下一针，「申脉」；脚踝前头那道横纹上、两条筋腱中间一针，「解溪」。「要是不赶着下课，外踝尖往上三寸还该加一个，悬钟。四针围着肿，手法轻，不补不泻。」

沈芒龇着牙，脑门上出了汗。老蔡在人堆里小声说：「忙哥，你这脚踝现在像个仙人掌。」

严老师头也不抬：「仙人掌不疼。他疼。」

留针的几分钟，他对着围着的一圈人说：「针能消肿，能止疼，能帮着那一带的血走一走。」他拔了针，拿棉球按住，「它不能让这根韧带长得快一天。疼和伤，是两本账。你那根筋，得它自己长。礼拜六的比赛，你别上了。」

沈芒从床上坐起来，试着把脚踝转了一圈，比上床前松了一点，疼也轻了一点。他这辈子头一回让严老师扎了一回针，针是真扎了，脚踝也真松了，严老师说的偏偏还是那句：你的主意不灵。

那天晚上，阿禾在一楼宿管阿姨那儿押了学生证，上六楼来六一七送绷带。

她把绷带往桌上一放，先看了一眼他的脚踝：「消了点。」

「严老师扎的。」

「扎能消肿。」阿禾说，「校医说几个月？」

「三个月。可他说一两个礼拜就不疼了。」

「不疼了，不等于长好了。」阿禾说，「韧带长得慢，比肉慢多了。」她抬起一只脚，闭上眼，单脚站着，纹丝不动，像一根钉在水泥地上的桩子，「崴过脚的，都得练这个。」

「站着就能长？」

「站着练的不是韧带，是线。」阿禾睁开眼，「你脚踝上有一堆报信的小东西，一刻不停地告诉脑子：脚往哪边歪了，歪了多少。一崴，这些线也扯断了一批。线断了，脑子不知道脚踩在哪儿，所以崴过一回的脚，最容易再崴。闭着眼站，脑子看不见，只能听脚上的线说话——听得多了，它就重新学会听了。每天闭着眼单脚站，站到一分钟不晃。」

他扶着桌沿试了一回。一闭眼，整个人像插在烂泥里的竹竿，两只胳膊乱划，第三秒上，好脚「啪」地踩实了地。

「三秒。」阿禾说。

老蔡在上铺探出头：「我数着呢。三秒，一秒不多。」

「礼拜六第三轮，」阿禾把本子夹在胳膊底下，「你站稳三十秒再说。」她走到门口，又回头，「我本子上写了一行。」

她没说写的什么。沈芒也没敢问。
story.en:
At eleven o'clock on the night of November 25th, Shen Mang stood looking at a cola-coloured puddle of urine in the toilet bowl, and his first thought was not "I'm going to die." It was: Ahe must not find out.

He had said that same sentence to himself once already, four days earlier.

November 14th, Saturday, round two of the group stage: Acupuncture-Tuina against Nursing.

Halfway through the second quarter, Ahe turned a page of her notebook behind the scorer's table and said something to Xing Bin, the captain. Xing Bin waved at the bench: "Number Zero."

Five minutes. She was as good as her word.

His legs were soft when he stood up; once he was on the court they stopped being soft — the Nursing players were all taller than him, but they played as if they were more afraid of the ball than he was. For the first two minutes he followed the ball wherever it went, like a dog chasing its own tail. In the third minute Nursing's tallest player shot from around the free-throw line, and the ball hit the back of the rim and bounced high.

A crowd of people under the basket jumped at once. Shen Mang jumped too. He didn't know where the nerve came from — he jumped with a pack of people half a head taller than him, both hands reaching for the sky — and the ball actually hit his hands. He pulled it into his chest.

The first rebound of his cup career.

When he came down, his right foot did not land on the floorboards. It landed on the tall player's instep. The ankle rolled outward with a "crack" he heard himself.

Then the pain. It went white in front of his eyes, and he sat down on the floor hugging the ball. He kept the ball locked in his arms; whoever tried to pry it loose, he would not let go. Pain or no pain, something in his chest was burning, burning hard enough to push tears up — he'd got it. The first rebound of the cup belonged to Number Zero. He looked over at the scorer's table: Ahe had her head down, writing, and didn't look at him.

Tuina beat Nursing by nine that day. He didn't see the final whistle — Ahe had two substitutes carry him straight to the school clinic by the gate, and she followed behind with her notebook under her arm.

The clinic doctor pressed the ankle, pressed the edge of the outer ankle bone, and had him walk four steps along the wall: "The bone doesn't hurt much to the touch, so no X-ray for now. The outer ligament is sprained." He prescribed an ankle brace and a pair of crutches. Shen Mang asked, "How many days till it's better?" The doctor said, "A week or two and it'll stop hurting. To heal properly, three months at least."

He heard only the first half: the third round was a week away, and once it stopped hurting he could play.

Ahe heard the second half. She asked the doctor: "Ice it the first few days or not? How many days before he can put weight on it? Should he get the X-ray?" When she had asked every question, she wrote a line in her notebook. Outside the clinic Shen Mang caught up with her on his crutches: "The third round—"

"The doctor said three months," Ahe said. "I've written it down."

He wanted to ask what she had written. The crutch slipped on the step first.

November 17th, Tuesday morning, third floor of the laboratory building: the acupuncture practical.

Teacher Yan's white coat was buttoned to the very top as always. The timetable said it plainly: "Locating points and filiform-needle practice (Zusanli)." In pairs: first find the point on your own leg; needles go into paper pads and cotton balls, never into a person, to train the fingers and the insertion; at the end Teacher Yan would ask for a volunteer and demonstrate one needle at Zusanli on a real leg.

Shen Mang came in on his crutches with an idea tucked inside him. Wasn't acupuncture meant for exactly this? The sign outside the tuina department at the school clinic said "ankle sprain" in plain characters. When Teacher Yan asked for a volunteer, he would be the first to raise his hand; the needle would go in, and maybe the ankle would clear along with it, and he'd be on the court by Saturday.

He was paired with Old Cai.

Teacher Yan taught the location first: the hollow below the kneecap on the outer side, three cun down, one finger-breadth out from the front edge of the shinbone. The whole class bent over their own legs, feeling about with a chorus of "ow". Shen Mang couldn't memorise a book, but this he could find — he pressed his finger on the strip of muscle outside the shinbone, hooked his toes up, and the muscle bulged under his finger. The anatomy course had a name for it: tibialis anterior. The point sat right on that muscle, with a nerve and a vessel running past underneath. It struck him suddenly that these points hadn't all fallen out of the sky: a good many sat where nerves and vessels passed, or in the seams between muscles — things a hand could actually feel.

"Zusanli, the He-sea point of the Stomach channel." Teacher Yan tapped the leg drawn on the blackboard with his chalk. "From fingertips and toes up to the elbow and knee, each channel has five key points in a row: Jing-well, Ying-spring, Shu-stream, Jing-river, He-sea. Like water welling up from a spring, running into a ditch, gathering into a river, and finally reaching the sea. He is where it reaches the sea. Why they're arranged that way, you'll hear in detail next term in Channels and Points."

Old Cai looked down at his own calf: "There's a sea in my leg?"

The class laughed. Teacher Yan didn't laugh and didn't scold; he handed out needles. The paper pad was a stack of coarse paper tied tight with string: pinch the handle and twist it in, turn by turn; once through, switch to the cotton ball and practise going in fast and straight. Across from him Old Cai held a needle in a hand that shook as if it were making the tip dance, twisted for half a day, and bent the needle into a bow on the pad. Shen Mang's needle, at least, went in straight — he had watched a month of needling videos on his phone, and his hands had something of the shape.

At the end Teacher Yan said: "Who'll come up?"

Shen Mang's hand was the first up. He got onto the examination couch on his crutches and rolled up his trouser leg. Teacher Yan swabbed the spot, and the needle went in faster than he could see. A soreness in the leg, then a swelling, then a numbness he couldn't name, running down the calf.

"Deqi — the arrival of qi," Teacher Yan told the class. "Sore, swollen, numb, travelling downward. That is what needling is after."

Old Cai's eyes were shining: "Mang! What does it feel like?"

"Sore."

The second hand up was Old Cai's. He said he had to feel it for himself. He sat on the couch; the needle had barely touched his skin when his face went white, a film of cold sweat on his forehead, his body went slack, and he toppled sideways. Teacher Yan was there in a stride, laid him flat, propped his legs up, opened a window, sent for sugar water. A few minutes later the colour came back into Old Cai's face, and lying on the edge of the couch he said weakly: "...I didn't have breakfast."

"Needle faint," Teacher Yan told the class. "Empty stomach, tired, nervous — the easiest way to get it. So eat before you're needled, and lying down is steadier than sitting up." That was the textbook, recited word for word; then he added a sentence the book didn't have: "When you needle your patients one day, the same applies."

Before the bell, Shen Mang edged up to the lectern on his crutches, rolled up his trouser leg, and showed an ankle swollen like a steamed bun: "Teacher Yan, could you put two needles in here? Could I play on Saturday?"

Teacher Yan looked for a while and didn't answer at once. He turned and wrote a line on the board: "What is called a node is where the spirit-qi travels and goes in and out; it is not skin, flesh, sinew or bone." He read it off with the stub of chalk: "First chapter of the Lingshu. A node is what later came to be called a point. The ancients say it isn't skin, flesh, sinew or bone — it's where the spirit-qi goes in and out. What spirit-qi is, the book doesn't say, and I won't write it in for them."

Shen Mang's finger was still pressed on his calf. The book said not flesh; under his finger it was plainly flesh.

"Needling does help with some kinds of pain." Teacher Yan closed the textbook. "But people have compared real needles with sham ones that never go in, and the gap is often small. Why it works, there are several theories, none of them settled." He checked his watch — ten minutes to the bell. "Lie down. I'll show you all."

The whole class crowded round in a rush. Shen Mang lay on the couch with his trouser leg rolled to the knee. Teacher Yan didn't touch the ankle. He picked up Shen Mang's left hand first.

"The right ankle is sprained, so I start on the left wrist." He pressed his thumb into the middle of the crease on the back of the wrist. "Yangchi, on the Sanjiao channel of the hand. The wrist answers to the ankle — this joint on the hand matches that one on the foot. The old rule is: left for a right-side illness. One needle far away first; the place that hurts, I leave alone." Swab, needle in; Shen Mang hissed. "Sore?" "Sore." "Keep it sore. Now turn the right ankle in slow circles. Not fast. Stop if it hurts."

Lying there with the swollen ankle propped up, Shen Mang turned it round and round. The first circles were like turning a rusty lock; by the seventh or eighth, the grit inside the lock eased, just a little. He felt it himself, and it must have shown on his face, because Teacher Yan nodded: "The needle stays in while you move — that's called motion needling. The effect is just this much. It isn't holy water."

The needle came out. Only then did Teacher Yan look down at the ankle, two fingers measuring across the swelling without touching it: "In front of and below the outer ankle bone, where it's swollen highest, is the anterior talofibular ligament; eight sprains in ten tear that one. While it's swollen, I don't go into it. I go around it." He set the needles as he talked, all shallow, a couple of twists and stop: one in the hollow in front of and below the outer ankle bone — "Qiuxu"; one in the dip behind it, in front of the Achilles tendon — "Kunlun"; one straight below the bone — "Shenmai"; one on the front crease of the ankle, between the two tendons — "Jiexi". "If we weren't racing the bell I'd add one more, three cun above the tip of the outer ankle bone: Xuanzhong. Four needles around the swelling, light hands, neither reinforcing nor reducing."

Shen Mang bared his teeth, sweat on his forehead. From the crowd Old Cai said under his breath: "Mang, your ankle looks like a cactus."

Teacher Yan didn't look up: "A cactus doesn't hurt. He does."

During the few minutes the needles stayed in, he spoke to the ring of faces: "Needles can bring swelling down, ease pain, and help the blood move through the area." He drew them out and pressed a cotton ball on each spot. "They cannot make this ligament grow one day faster. Pain and injury are two separate accounts. That ligament has to grow on its own. Saturday — you don't play."

Shen Mang sat up and tried turning the ankle: a little looser than before he lay down, a little less pain. For the first time in his life Teacher Yan had put needles in him — real needles, and the ankle really had loosened — and what Teacher Yan had said was still, of all things: your idea won't work.

That evening Ahe left her student card with the dorm auntie on the ground floor and climbed to 617 on the sixth to bring bandages.

She put the bandages on the desk and looked at his ankle first: "It's gone down a bit."

"Teacher Yan needled it."

"Needles bring swelling down," Ahe said. "How many months did the doctor say?"

"Three. But he said it'd stop hurting in a week or two."

"Not hurting isn't the same as healed," Ahe said. "Ligaments grow slowly — far slower than muscle." She lifted one foot, closed her eyes, and stood on the other without a tremor, like a post driven into the concrete floor. "Everyone who's sprained an ankle has to do this."

"Standing makes it grow?"

"Standing doesn't train the ligament. It trains the wires." Ahe opened her eyes. "You've got a heap of little messengers around that ankle, telling your brain all day long which way the foot is tilting and by how much. A sprain tears a batch of those wires too. With the wires cut, the brain doesn't know where the foot is — that's why a sprained ankle is the easiest to sprain again. Stand with your eyes shut and the brain can't see; all it can do is listen to the wires in the foot. Listen enough, and it learns to hear them again. Every day, one foot, eyes closed, until you can hold a minute without swaying."

He held the edge of the desk and tried. The moment he shut his eyes his whole body became a bamboo pole stuck in mud, arms flailing, and on the third second the good foot slapped down flat on the floor.

"Three seconds," Ahe said.

Old Cai poked his head out from the top bunk: "I was counting. Three seconds, not one more."

"Round three on Saturday," Ahe tucked the notebook under her arm, "hold thirty seconds first, then we'll talk." At the door she turned back. "I've written a line in my book."

She didn't say what. Shen Mang didn't dare ask.
